name: Djibouti
summary_text: Djibouti is dangerous for trans visitors. The penal code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex conduct, but vague “good morals” provisions (Arts 353/354) make homosexuality “de facto illegal” in practice; no anti-discrimination law, no LGR, no community infrastructure; authoritarian state with US/French bases but no rights space.

sources.title: Djibouti | Outright International
sources.claim_summary: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Djibouti's penal code does not explicitly criminalise LGBTIQ identities or consensual same-sex conduct, but Sections 353-354 refer vaguely to 'good morals'; homosexuality is regarded as de facto illegal. No anti-discrimination law; the 2023 US State Department report found pervasive social and religious intolerance and fear of assembly; no LGBTIQ organisations identified.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Djibouti - Wikipedia
sources.claim_summary: Wikipedia overview: legality of same-sex activity is ambiguous (no law explicitly criminalising it, but 'obscene acts' provisions); limited protection based on sexual orientation; no gender-identity recognition; LGBTQ people face stigmatisation.

sources.title: Djibouti - United States Department of State
sources.claim_summary: US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Djibouti: official assessment including the SOGI section - pervasive social and religious intolerance, LGBTIQ persons afraid to assemble or express themselves, no known prosecutions.

US State Department 2015 Human Rights Report for Djibouti: general human-rights assessment (suppression of opposition, harsh prisons, FGM, trafficking) - baseline context with limited LGBT-specific content.

sources.title: IRB – Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada (Autor): „Djibouti: Treatment of sexual minorities, including legislation, state protection, and support services (2009-March 2012) [D
sources.claim_summary: Canadian IRB Response to Information Request DJI104070.E (2012): treatment of sexual minorities in Djibouti (2009-March 2012) - information scarce; societal norms did not allow public discussion of homosexuality; GlobalGayz reports gay people 'living undercover and in fear' with 'virtually zero tolerance'; but no known reports of societal violence or discrimination; legislation ambiguous (some sources say illegal, ILGA says not criminalised).
